"'In other words, if we have a point 'P' in n-dimensional space, and we want to project it onto a subspace spanned by two basis vectors 'v' and 'w', then the projection of 'P' onto 'v' will only be accurate if 'v' and 'w' are orthogonal to each other,' explained Dr. Jane Doe, a leading researcher in the field.

If 'v' and 'w' are not orthogonal, then the dot product 'P' · 'w' will not be zero, and the projection of 'P' onto 'v' will not be accurate,' said Dr. Smith.

"'However, if 'v' and 'w' are orthogonal, then the dot product 'P' · 'w' will be zero, and the projection of 'P' onto 'v' will be accurate. This is why orthogonal projection is a powerful tool for reducing the dimensionality of a vector space and for finding the closest approximation of a point to a subspace,' said Dr. Doe.

"'In summary, orthogonal projection only works if the two basis vectors 'v' are orthogonal to each other. If they are not, then the projection of a point onto 'v' will not be accurate,' concluded Dr. Smith."
